***

As December approaches, shops across Britain are stocking their shelves with an increasingly elaborate array of advent calendars. Gone are the days when a simple cardboard calendar with tiny milk chocolate shapes behind each door would suffice. Today's offerings range from luxury beauty products worth hundreds of pounds to artisanal gin collections and even pet treat calendars for the family dog. Yet despite this explosion of choice, chocolate advent calendars remain the nation's favourite, with over 16 million sold in the UK last year alone.

***

The tradition of advent calendars dates back to 19th century Germany, where families would mark the days leading up to Christmas with chalk lines on the wall or by lighting candles. The first printed advent calendar appeared in 1908, but it wasn't until the 1950s that chocolates were added behind the little doors. What began as a simple religious countdown for children has evolved into a multi-million pound industry that appeals to all ages and tastes.

***

This year's chocolate offerings span from budget-friendly supermarket own-brands at under £1 to premium Belgian truffle collections exceeding £50. Thorntons has released a calendar featuring miniature versions of their classic Continental selection, while Hotel Chocolat's offering includes everything from salted caramel puddles to gin-infused truffles. Even traditionally non-chocolate brands have entered the fray, with Kellogg's creating a calendar filled with white chocolate pieces shaped like tiny Crunchy Nut Cornflakes.

***

However, the boom in advent calendar variety hasn't been without controversy. Environmental campaigners have raised concerns about the excessive packaging, particularly in beauty calendars that can contain more plastic than product. Meanwhile, parents worry about the commercialisation of what was once a simple Christmas tradition, with some calendars now costing more than many families spend on actual Christmas presents. Despite these concerns, the advent calendar industry shows no signs of slowing, with retailers already reporting record pre-orders for next year's editions before this December has even begun.
